title: What Medicare Open Enrollment Plan Changes Can Mean for Your Pharmacy and Patients
body_markdown:
January can bring more than a new year for Medicare patients. It can also mean a new deductible, a higher copay, or an unexpected change at the pharmacy counter.


‍


Many of those changes begin taking shape earlier, during Medicare Open Enrollment, which runs from October through early December. During this period, patients can review their prescription drug coverage and make changes that take effect January 1.


‍


For independent pharmacies, Open Enrollment is an important opportunity to help patients understand what’s changing, keep prescriptions from going elsewhere, and prepare your team for the year ahead. With the right approach, your pharmacy can turn a potentially confusing time for patients into an opportunity to strengthen relationships and provide valuable guidance.


‍


## **What matters during Medicare Open Enrollment**


‍


Medicare Open Enrollment runs from October 15 through December 7, and changes take effect January 1. For pharmacies, the biggest day-to-day impact often comes through Part D: a plan may change which medications it covers, what patients pay, or which pharmacies are in network.


‍


Patients can switch drug plans, join or leave Medicare Advantage, or keep their current coverage. If they do nothing, their plan generally renews automatically, but that does not mean the details will stay the same. Some patients may not discover a change until a claim is rejected in January, a prescription costs more, or they learn their pharmacy is out of network.


‍


## **Why plan changes matter at the pharmacy**


‍


A change in coverage can affect both where a prescription is filled and what a patient pays. New deductibles, updated insurance cards, and rejected claims can also bring more questions and extra work for pharmacy teams in January.


‍


When the cost at pickup is higher than expected, patients may delay a refill or leave a prescription behind. That can disrupt care and add pressure during an already busy month. Patients taking high-cost or complex medications, including GLP-1s, may be especially affected by changes to coverage or out-of-pocket costs.


‍


## **Help patients understand their options**


‍


Pharmacists are among the most trusted sources of help for Medicare patients, and everyday conversations can surface when a plan may no longer fit a patient’s medications or budget. Raising the issue before January gives patients more time to compare options and avoid surprises at the counter. It also shows them your pharmacy is looking out for them, building trust and strengthening loyalty.


‍


Keep the conversation simple and specific. For example: “Your plan may change what you pay for this medication in January. Let’s look at your options.”


‍


You can help patients:


- Compare plans and medications with[Medicare Plan Compare](https://www.medicare.gov/plan-compare/)


- Check whether a medication will remain covered and what it may cost


- Confirm whether your pharmacy is in the plan’s network


- Compare total prescription costs, since a lower premium does not always mean lower costs at the pharmacy


- Find programs that may help with medication costs


‍


## **Get your team ready for January**


‍


A little preparation now can make coverage questions easier to handle after the new year. Consider reviewing patients with high-cost or complex prescriptions and flagging those who may need a conversation. Remind Medicare patients of the December 7 deadline through text, email, or your usual outreach, and prepare staff for new insurance cards, coverage questions, and claim rejections.


‍


It also helps to set expectations about deductibles and possible changes in out-of-pocket costs. Make pickup and payment as straightforward as possible, so cost or confusion is less likely to keep a prescription from being picked up.


‍
